speech: Friday, 4:45 pm. The client report is still a blank page.
li:
Client reports are the most common thing that eats an agency's Friday. The numbers live in five tools and the layout never changes.

That is a good job to hand off: an assistant pulls the numbers into your template, you review and send. Start with one client for one month and see how many hours come back.
x: Agency owners: the client report that eats your Friday is a repeat task. Hand off the number-pulling, keep the review.

speech: The work is done. The invoice is not paid. Nobody has asked.
li:
Some late payments are simply unsent reminders. A polite email on day 1, day 7 and day 14 is a simple routine, yet it rarely gets done because it feels small.

Small, repeat and written is exactly what a virtual assistant does well. You keep the relationship, they keep the calendar of reminders.
x: Many late invoices are just unsent reminders. A day 1, 7 and 14 email routine is easy to hand off.

speech: Three showings, two time zones, one very full calendar.
li:
Real estate teams lose agent hours to scheduling, listing updates and CRM entry. None of it needs a licence, and all of it follows a checklist.

Hand those tasks off and agents spend the hours on clients. Our assistants work in your time zone on non-calling tasks.
x: Scheduling, listing updates and CRM entry follow a checklist. Hand them off so agents spend hours on clients.

speech: Owner statements are due. So are 40 tenant emails.
li:
Property managers spend a lot of time on tenant emails, maintenance tracking and owner statements. The repeat parts can be handed off with a clear checklist.

What cannot be handed off: emergencies, entry to units and legal decisions. Keep those with your on-call team.
x: Tenant emails, maintenance logs and owner statements repeat every month. Hand off the repeat parts, keep emergencies in-house.

speech: Day 12 of asking a client for the same bank statement.
li:
Document chasing is the quiet cost in every accounting practice. Each reminder is small, but together they steal partner and senior hours.

An assistant can send reminders, track what has arrived and keep a deadline list. Tax advice and filings stay with your qualified team.
x: Chasing client documents steals senior hours. Reminders and tracking are easy to hand off. Advice and filings stay with you.

speech: Intake forms, calendar invites and billing prep. Again.
li:
Law firms can hand off intake admin, scheduling and billing preparation with strict limits: no legal advice, no handling of client funds, and clear confidentiality terms.

Start with one repeat task and keep the access narrow.
x: Intake admin, scheduling and billing prep can be handed off with strict limits. No legal advice, narrow access.

speech: Inbox zero is a story people tell at conferences.
li:
If email is the first thing you open and the last thing you close, it is a hand-off candidate. Sorting, flagging and drafting routine replies follows rules you can write down in one page.

A free plan shows what to hand off first, week by week.
x: If email is the first thing you open and the last thing you close, it is a hand-off candidate. A free plan shows where to start.

speech: 160 hours a month. One person who knows your work.
li:
A dedicated virtual assistant works your hours on your tasks every month. The full-time plan is 160 hours for $899, which is $5.62 an hour. Part-time is 80 hours for $500.

It fits steady work that fills the month. If your work is lighter, start with a small block instead.
x: Full-time dedicated virtual assistant: 160 hours for $899, or $5.62 an hour. Part-time is 80 hours for $500.

speech: A 15-minute task. What does it actually cost?
li:
Cost per task is simple: minutes divided by 60, times the hourly rate. A 15-minute task at $5.62 an hour is $1.40. At the $12 pay-as-you-go rate it is $3.00.

The guide has the full table by plan, plus example tasks with the assumed minutes shown.
x: A 15-minute task costs $1.40 at $5.62 an hour and $3.00 at $12 an hour. Cost per task is minutes divided by 60 times the rate.

speech: Which plan? Add your repeat jobs, divide by 60.
li:
To pick a plan, list your repeat jobs, note the minutes each takes, add them up and divide by 60. Under 5 hours a month suits a small block or pay-as-you-go. Work that fills the month suits the 160-hour plan.

Unused hours roll over while your account is active.
x: Pick a plan in 3 steps: list repeat jobs, add the minutes, divide by 60. Unused hours roll over.

speech: Guest asks about the Wi-Fi at 2 am. Again.
li: Hosts answer the same ten guest questions all year. Saved answers, a calendar check and a cleaner schedule are easy to hand off. Keys, cleaning and emergencies stay with you or a local co-host.
x: Hosts answer the same ten guest questions all year. Save the answers, hand off the replies, keep the keys.

speech: The books are 'fine'. Nobody has looked since March.
li: Early books are simple but they pile up. A separate business bank account, a receipt habit and a monthly routine keep them clean. A 30-day plan in the guide shows the order. This is record keeping, not tax advice, so keep an accountant for advice and filings.
x: Early books pile up fast. A 30-day setup plan: bank account, receipts, monthly routine. Keep an accountant for advice.

speech: Month-end close in 12 steps. Step 6 holds up the rest.
li: Reconciling the bank is the step that protects every other step in a month-end close. The checklist has all 12 steps and a hand-off table showing what a VA can do and what stays with your accountant.
x: Month-end close in 12 steps. Step 6, reconcile the bank, protects the other eleven.

speech: Day one with a new assistant. Where do I even start?
li: The first week sets the pattern. Pick three repeat jobs, write one brief for each, review the first results and save your feedback as a checklist. The onboarding checklist has the full list.
x: First week with an assistant: pick 3 repeat jobs, write one brief each, review, save feedback as a checklist.

speech: A good brief fits on one page. Most fit on three lines.
li: Most delegation problems are brief problems. A short brief with the goal, the steps, an example and the deadline gets better work than a long call. There is a free fill-in template.
x: Most delegation problems are brief problems. Goal, steps, example, deadline. Free template.

speech: AI drafts fast. Someone still has to check it.
li: AI is fast at drafts, lists and first passes. A person decides what is right for your business. The guide compares a virtual assistant and an AI assistant task by task, including where AI alone is the better pick.
x: AI drafts fast. A person decides what is right for your business. A task-by-task comparison.

speech: Salary, tax, desk, software. Then a sick day.
li: Compare the true cost of a local hire with a virtual assistant using your own numbers. Enter your hours, your local rate and your extra costs, and the calculator shows both side by side.
x: Compare a local hire with a virtual assistant using your own numbers. Free calculator.

speech: 9 am in London is 2:30 pm in Kerala. Plan around it.
li: Time zone overlap matters more than the hourly rate. Our team works from Kerala, India and plans shifts around your working day. The free planner shows the overlap for your city, with daylight saving handled.
x: Time zone overlap matters more than the hourly rate. A free planner shows the overlap for your city.

speech: Not sure yet? Try 3 hours first.
li: If you have never delegated before, test with real work. The free 3-hour trial runs for 2 days. You choose the plan you continue with, and that plan starts after the trial. Prices are in US dollars.
x: Try 3 hours free first. The trial runs for 2 days, then the plan you choose starts.

speech: Hours in, cheapest plan out. No sign-up.
li: Enter your hours per month and the calculator shows the cheapest plan across pay-as-you-go, blocks, quarterly packs and the dedicated plans. It works without signing up.
x: Hours in, cheapest plan out. Free calculator, no sign-up.

speech: Ten questions to ask before you pay anyone.
li: Before you pay any virtual assistant provider, check ten things: task scope, quality review, response time, cover for absence, pricing, rollover, contract, tool access, communication and a paid test. The checklist has the questions.
x: Ten things to check before you pay any virtual assistant provider. Free checklist.

speech: Job board, marketplace, agency or managed service?
li: The four ways to hire a virtual assistant trade price, control and effort differently. The guide compares them in one table with no provider names, so you can decide what fits before you start talking to anyone.
x: Job board, marketplace, agency or managed service? One table compares the four ways to hire.

speech: The cheapest hourly rate is not the cheapest bill.
li: Count rework, training time and cover for absence before you compare hourly rates. The guide lists the hidden costs and seven ways to lower the bill without lowering the quality.
x: The cheapest hourly rate is not the cheapest bill. Count rework, training and cover.

speech: Orders, returns and 'where is my parcel?' emails.
li: Online store owners spend hours on listings, orders and customer messages. Most follow written rules. Hand off the repeat parts and keep pricing and policy decisions with you.
x: Listings, orders and customer messages follow written rules. Hand off the repeat parts, keep the decisions.
